content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has updated its recommendations for the prevention and control of influenza, as outlined by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). These updates reflect the latest evidence and epidemiological data regarding influenza vaccination and antiviral use. Influenza epidemics in the United States typically occur annually during late fall through early spring. Influenza viruses can infect individuals across all age groups, but children experience the highest rates of infection. However, the risk of severe illness and death is greatest among individuals aged 65 years and older, children younger than 5 years, and individuals with underlying medical conditions that predispose them to complications. During the 2009 influenza A (H1N1) pandemic, the majority of circulating influenza viruses were the pandemic H1N1 strain. Epidemiological studies from this period revealed that adults aged 19–64 years faced a higher risk of complications from H1N1 infection compared to typical seasonal influenza. The pandemic H1N1 virus is expected to continue circulating during future influenza seasons, but it remains uncertain whether it will replace or co-circulate with other seasonal influenza A subtypes, such as H1N1 and H3N2, which have been circulating since 1977. The extent of antigenic drift and evolution of the pandemic H1N1 strain in the future is unpredictable. Annual influenza vaccination remains the most effective strategy for preventing influenza virus infection and its complications. Vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older who do not have contraindications. Trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (TIV) is suitable for individuals aged 6 months and older, including those with high-risk conditions. Live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) may be used for healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2–49 years. No preference is given between LAIV and TIV for healthy, non-pregnant individuals in this age group. However, individuals with underlying medical conditions that increase their risk for influenza complications should only receive TIV, as the safety and efficacy of LAIV in these populations have not been established. Despite recent increases in vaccination coverage among certain groups, significant gaps remain, and efforts to improve vaccination rates in both medical and non-medical settings should be expanded. Antiviral medications serve as an adjunct to vaccination and are effective when used for treatment or chemoprophylaxis following exposure to influenza. However, the emergence of antiviral resistance among circulating strains since 2005 has complicated treatment and prophylaxis recommendations. The CDC periodically revises its antiviral guidelines based on resistance patterns and risk factors for complications. The ACIP provides annual recommendations for influenza prevention and control. The ACIP Influenza Work Group meets regularly to review new studies, update guidelines, and consider revisions. The group evaluates factors such as disease burden, vaccine effectiveness and safety, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and anticipated vaccine supply. Recommendations are based on high-quality, peer-reviewed studies, with additional input from unpublished but relevant data. Randomized controlled trials assessing laboratory-confirmed influenza outcomes provide the strongest evidence for vaccine and antiviral efficacy, but observational studies also contribute valuable safety and effectiveness data, particularly in populations where vaccination is already recommended. The 2010 ACIP recommendations include several key updates: 1. Routine influenza vaccination is now recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older. This expansion is supported by evidence demonstrating the safety and effectiveness of annual vaccination across all age groups. 2. Vaccination efforts should continue to prioritize individuals at higher risk for influenza-related complications, even as the transition to universal vaccination occurs. 3. In situations of limited vaccine supply, priority should be given to high-risk groups, including young children, older adults, individuals with chronic medical conditions, pregnant women, and healthcare personnel. 4. New and expanded age indications for certain inactivated influenza vaccines have been approved, including Fluvirin for individuals aged 4 years and older, and Afluria for individuals aged 6 months and older. Influenza A and B viruses are responsible for human epidemics. Influenza A viruses are further categorized into subtypes based on hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) surface antigens. Antigenic drift, caused by point mutations during viral replication, leads to the emergence of new variants and necessitates annual updates to vaccine strains. Antigenic shift, which involves the appearance of a novel influenza A subtype, can result in pandemics when there is little or no pre-existing immunity in the population. The 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus originated from swine influenza viruses and is antigenically distinct from human H1N1 viruses that have circulated since 1977. It contains a unique combination of gene segments not previously reported in humans or animals. The HA gene of the pandemic H1N1 virus is closely related to that of contemporary swine influenza viruses and is thought to have evolved from the avian-origin 1918 pandemic H1N1 virus. Influenza-related hospitalizations and deaths vary by age and underlying health status. Children under 5 years, particularly those under 2 years, experience higher rates of hospitalization compared to older children. During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, hospitalization and death rates among individuals under 65 years exceeded those observed during typical seasonal epidemics. Older adults, however, experienced lower rates of hospitalization and death, likely due to partial immunity from prior exposure to antigenically similar viruses. Influenza-associated deaths are uncommon among children, but the majority of pediatric deaths occur in children without known high-risk conditions. This underscores the importance of universal vaccination to protect all children, regardless of their health status.
